entry.title: Combined summary - Lichen: L2s In CHannels ENforced on bitcoin
entry.summary: The discussed email elaborates on a new transaction handling approach within Layer 2 (L2) networks, specifically focusing on co-owned contracts that eliminate the need for trust in the hub's operational integrity or liveness. This system enables users to manage and withdraw hub tokens as bitcoin via a multi-signature setup with the hub, ensuring transactions can still be processed directly on the Bitcoin blockchain even if the hub fails to act or goes offline. Importantly, this does not require any modifications to Bitcoin's existing consensus protocol. The technical aspects of handling disputed withdrawals are addressed using RISC Zero to demonstrate a withdrawal statement, which is then validated by Groth16—a cryptographic proof system. BitVMX supports this by facilitating an on-chain review process involving a RISC-V program, specifically a Groth16 verifier, to efficiently resolve disputes. This mechanism aims to preemptively settle most disputes within milliseconds through deterministic verifiability but is capable of engaging in a more extensive search when necessary. The L2 solution under discussion highlights the critical role of liquidity and the user’s ability to access funds easily, which significantly depends on the inbound liquidity from the hub. However, it also comes with inherent risks related to the finality of transactions and the types of operations supported by the L2 ledger. Despite potential vulnerabilities linked to its centralized nature, the model ensures each token issued by the hub is backed by actual reserve assets, facilitating redeemability without needing the hub's permission. The broader application possibilities of this L2 configuration extend to supporting high-privacy transactions and complex smart contracts across various hubs. For further understanding and potential implementation details, the [Lichen Draft Paper](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/papers/lichen-draft.pdf) provides comprehensive demonstrations and verification processes. Moreover, concerns about post-quantum vulnerabilities associated with deploying infrastructure like Groth16 within the Bitcoin ecosystem have been raised. Specifically, the susceptibility of the Common Reference String from RiscZero to quantum attacks could compromise system integrity by enabling forgeries, thereby placing funds at risk. Legal and confidentiality issues are also highlighted, with strict instructions against unauthorized use or dissemination of the information provided, emphasizing the sensitivity of the content. More details on these privacy policies can be found at [Anchorage's privacy policy page](https://www.anchorage.com/privacy-policy). In a separate discourse, the utility of integrating systems like Groth16 with Bitcoin is defended based on their ability to offer enhanced privacy and functionality without compromising the security assumptions stronger than those currently used by Bitcoin. This perspective suggests that such integrations are not only viable but necessary for advancing the capabilities of Bitcoin payment systems while maintaining user freedom and transaction efficiency.
